# Dog vs cat: what actually differs

*Generated by `demo.py`. The two workflows are the same code with different species configs; everything below is a measured difference between the two species, not a difference in method.*

## The molecule

**RIGOROUS** — UniProt reviewed mature chains, positional comparison.

| recipient | product | foreign residues | positions | non-self 9-mer cores |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| dog | human insulin | 1 | B30A>T | 1 |
| dog | bovine insulin | 2 | A8T>A, A10I>V | 10 |
| dog | pig insulin | 0 | — | 0 |
| cat | human insulin | 4 | A8A>T, A10V>I, A18H>N, B30A>T | 14 |
| cat | bovine insulin | 1 | A18H>N | 4 |
| cat | pig insulin | 3 | A8A>T, A10V>I, A18H>N | 13 |

Two things this table says that a residue count alone does not:

* **Porcine insulin is the dog's own molecule.** Zero differences, zero non-self cores — the only species/product pair here with nothing for an epitope screen to find. The cat has no equivalent; its closest natural match, bovine insulin, still differs at A18.
* **Where a difference sits matters more than how many there are.** The dog's single difference from human insulin is B30, the last residue of the B chain, and it generates exactly one non-self register. Bovine insulin's two differences sit at A8/A10, inside the A chain, and generate ten. Counting residues would rank these the other way round.

## The prediction infrastructure

**MEASURED** — panel construction and applicability-domain distances computed in this run.

| species | locus | training molecules | training 5th pct NN identity | panel median NN identity | out-of-domain |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| dog | DQA | 90 | 0.900 | 0.750 | 0/6 |
| dog | DQB | 449 | 0.870 | 0.730 | 1/6 |
| dog | DRB | 1718 | 0.880 | 0.680 | 18/24 |
| cat | DRB | 1718 | 0.880 | 0.609 | 22/22 |

The asymmetry is structural, not incidental:

* IPD-MHC maintains a curated canine DLA section under ISAG nomenclature. It has **no feline section at all**, so the FLA panel in this run had to be scraped from GenBank/RefSeq: no allele names, no curation, no denominator.
* Neither species has an allele-**frequency** database, so neither panel can be converted into a population-coverage percentage. The human convention of quoting "95–98% population coverage" has no analogue here for either animal.
* Every feline molecule lands outside NetMHCIIpan-4.3's training space; the canine panel is mostly outside it but has members close enough to call marginal. That is the honest ceiling on how much weight a binding score can carry in each species.

## Validation

| species | checks passed | failed | skipped |
|---|---|---|---|
| dog | 16/16 | none | none |
| cat | 15/16 | none | KAT-3 |

`KAT-3` is skipped for the cat and passes for the dog, and that single difference is the clearest statement of the whole comparison: the dog has a marketed insulin (porcine) that is sequence-identical to its own, so the identity control is a real product. No such control exists for the cat.

## Bottom line

**Dog** — a species-matched product has no T-cell epitope question to answer; put the analytical effort into aggregation, process impurities and PTMs. A human-sequence product raises a single, terminal, well-bounded register. Analogue chemistry (glargine's B31-B32 extension, the acyl chains on detemir and degludec) moves more mass than the species gap does.

**Cat** — four differences, three of them interior to the A chain, so the non-self registers are real and clustered at A8/A10/A18. That cluster is small enough to interrogate properly. But the FLA infrastructure will not support a quantitative population risk statement, so the defensible output is a ranked register-level hypothesis list, reported RUO, ideally read out in a feline PBMC assay against those specific A-chain peptides rather than argued from scores.

**Both** — the sequence-level analysis (section 1 of each report) is model-free and carries the regulatory weight. The binding layer is extrapolation with no species benchmark, and the workflow says so in every artefact it writes rather than in a footnote.
